podcast.body: "Bitter Sweet Symphony" was used in a Nike "I Can" campaign commercial, which debuted on January 11, 1998, during the NFC Championship. This occurred despite the song still being on the charts and against the band's wishes. The Verve had lost the copyright to the song to Abkco, the company that administered The Rolling Stones' work, following a legal challenge over excessive sampling from a Stones-related cover. Abkco then licensed the song to Nike without the band's consent, leading to significant disapproval from both The Verve and their fans. "Abco sued, got the rights to bittersweet symphony, and immediately licensed it to Nike."

podcast.body: This song is a very complex composition, featuring 50 distinct tracks. One track incorporates the famous five notes from an instrumental version of The Rolling Stones' "The Last Time" by Andrew Loog Oldham, for which The Verve had sought and received permission. The remaining 49 tracks were composed entirely by The Verve, and its lyrics were written by Richard Ashcroft. Despite this extensive original composition, the song became the subject of a highly complicated and controversial legal battle regarding its authorship and rights, eventually leading to The Verve losing all control over it. It achieved intergenerational success and generated significant income. The song was nominated for a Grammy for "Best Song of the Year," leading to Richard Ashcroft, Mick Jagger, and Keith Richards being nominated as composers, despite the complex legal situation. "Vitex y simple, es una canción muy compleja, tiene las 50 pistas de música de las cuales por un lado tenemos una pista con los 5 notas famosas de la canción instrumental de los Rolling Stones pero tenemos otras 49 pistas de sonido que fueron compuestas por de ver y luego tenemos la letra que es completamente escrita por Richard Ascro."

podcast.body: This song, intended as the band's big comeback single, features a 4.5-second sample from an obscure orchestral cover of The Rolling Stones' "The Last Time" from the mid-1960s. Despite initial permission requests to Mick Jagger, Keith Richards, and Andrew Loog Oldham being met with little concern, former Stones manager Allen Klein, who controlled the copyright to Stones songs up to 1970, refused sampling on principle. A deal was eventually struck where Klein would split royalties 50/50, but this meant 50% for Mick Jagger and 50% for Keith Richards, leaving The Verve with only a flat thousand dollars for the lyrics. "Much of Bitter Sweet Symphony is built around a 4.5 second sample from an orchestral version of a Rolling Stones song called The Last Time."

podcast.body: Written by Richard Ashcroft, this song was inspired by a five-note progression from Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra's 1965 cover of The Rolling Stones' "The Last Time." The Verve initially licensed the snippet from Abkco Music (controlled by Allen Klein) for 50% of the song's earnings. However, Abkco later sued, claiming more of the sample was used than agreed, and Andrew Loog Oldham also sued for $1.7 million in royalties. Under duress, The Verve surrendered 100% of the publishing to Abkco and Oldham, leading to the songwriting credits being changed to "Ashcroft Jagger Richards." Abkco subsequently licensed the recording to Nike for a TV commercial, which was seen as "selling out" and severely damaged the band's artistic integrity with their indie fanbase, despite it not being their decision. The song was nominated for a Grammy, with the songwriters listed as "Jagger Richards," and the original five-note bit was actually written by orchestral arranger David Whitaker. "Richard Ashcroft of the Verve came up with a song called Bittersweet Symphony."
